<reason>A genuinely close, high-quality clash. PRO built a coherent case that the harm is the engineered chase rather than the payout, answered both pressure questions honestly (conceding the corner shop needs no licence while distinguishing on delivery mechanics), and landed a sharp closing reversal turning CON's own "sham token" anti-avoidance principle against duplicate-to-dust conversion. But CON made the debate easier to decide: the "relabelling, not rescue" argument — that PRO's stated victory condition is the same child spending the same money on fixed-price skins now blessed as "ordinary commerce" — was never squarely neutralized, and CON's pressure question forcing PRO to name the harm exposed that PRO's case rests on the chance element alone while leaving the Fortnite-style wallet drain untouched. CON also drew a workable line between self-declared family-account age signalling and licence-grade identity verification, blunting PRO's "same machinery" attack, and offered consumer-protection regulators as an enforcer with teeth. CON's "PRO regulates the flip, I regulate the spending" frame was the cleanest decision rule on the table. PRO's four clipped turns (every speech) cost it its concluding sentences repeatedly and included a slightly brittle "tenth of a second that testing showed" claim. Razor-thin but real edge to CON.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 1 [A2.1]–[A2.3]: catching PRO calling Fortnite's fixed-price shop "ordinary commerce, handled by parental controls and refunds" and asking why those same controls are hopeless when a card flips but sufficient when it doesn't — reframing PRO's substitution "victory" as a relabelling that leaves the child's wallet identical. PRO's "bounded by wanting" answer was reasonable but CON's manufactured-scarcity reply kept the point live through the closing.</best_rebuttal>
